name: Brexit
seoDesc: Brexit: work out cost so far from the cost before 1/1/20 and the cost post 1/1/20. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Brexit calculator the cost before 1/1/20, the cost post 1/1/20, the total government spending and the ex-MP 'winding up' costs and it returns cost so far. That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Brexit calculator work?
sections.html:
The Brexit calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports cost so far in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you give the dates it asks for; then you type in the cost before 1/1/20, the cost post 1/1/20, the total government spending and the ex-MP 'winding up' costs.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Brexit calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Cost so far=(since referendum till..., cost before 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, cost post 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, total government spending, divorce bill, is the divorce bill justified?)
Meals for children=((1 ÷ 8) × (since referendum till..., cost before 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, cost post 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, total government spending, divorce bill, is the divorce bill justified?))
Hospitals=((1 ÷ 90000000) × (since referendum till..., cost before 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, cost post 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, total government spending, divorce bill, is the divorce bill justified?))
Large wind turbines=((1 ÷ 3130000) × (since referendum till..., cost before 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, cost post 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, total government spending, divorce bill, is the divorce bill justified?))
Police officers=((1 ÷ 798840) × (since referendum till..., cost before 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, cost post 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, total government spending, divorce bill, is the divorce bill justified?))
Miles of HS2=((1 ÷ 403000000) × (since referendum till..., cost before 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, cost post 1 ÷ 1 ÷ 20, total government spending, divorce bill, is the divorce bill justified?))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Time, opening in weeks
  • Time, opening in weeks
  • Time, opening in weeks

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Brexit calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the cost before 1/1/20, the cost post 1/1/20 and the total government spending — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Brexit calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns cost so far, derived from the cost before 1/1/20, the cost post 1/1/20 and the total government spending. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Brexit calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the cost before 1/1/20, the cost post 1/1/20, the total government spending and the ex-MP 'winding up' costs, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter current cost in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Current cost opens in weeks and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Total government spending = 6870550000. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Brexit calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
